claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: either we can go through charts and mark the patterns based on discretion, or we can do it with a rule set and probably let a computer mark them. The first of those choices is subject to a massive amount of error and influence from the researcher.

claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: Even some of the best-known 'encyclopedias' of technical patterns show patterns that have never failed, that are 100% reliable. This, of course, is impossible - markets do not work like that. ... work done like this is potentially highly misleading.
claims.source_failure_or_counterexample_anchor: Counterexample to pattern encyclopedias that claim 100% reliability.

claims.source_context_note: Same section. Acknowledges that some patterns are context-dependent and resist simple quantification while still being real to a discretionary trader.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: Some patterns may depend on complex factors such as time of day, action (or volatility) in related markets, and other aspects of context. ... some patterns can't be explained in a simple rule set.

claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: you need to compare to a baseline drawn from the asset itself. Your comparison is not zero. ... if you have an active trading system that is long-only stocks and ... returns about 6% a year over a long slice of data. Great, but the buy and hold return might have been 7% or 8%. Does your approach even have an edge? (Probably not.)
claims.source_no_trade_if_explicit: Implied: do not actively trade an approach that does not beat the asset baseline after risk considerations.

claims.ambiguity_notes: The source does not define which context factors to quantify; that remains an open interpretation/operationalization question.
claims.source_context_note: Section 'Can the whole be more than the sum of the parts?'. Source argues context must be quantified rather than used to dismiss statistical results.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: Technical traders are guilty of saying 'context' and dismissing everything ... 'You have to put it in context, of course. Of course a statistical test will show it doesn't work, because you must have context.' If this is true, quantifying aspects of this context isn't just crucial - it's non-negotiable. ... 'context' can be the refuge of a trader that doesn't want to do the work to quantify an edge.

claims.source_context_note: One of the author's bullets explaining why he abandoned Fibonacci levels. Combines live-trade observation with a confluence critique.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: You couldn't be sure which level would work, but some level always worked after the fact. I began to realize that levels would be violated in live trades; I had dutifully placed my stop a few ticks beyond, but then another level clearly held at the end of the day. There was no way, and no way in the literature, to predict which level would hold. ... we were drawing so many levels on charts that it might just be luck that they seemed to work.
claims.source_exit_or_management_if_explicit: Example: stops placed a few ticks beyond a level were violated; another level held instead.
claims.source_invalidation_if_explicit: Levels being violated in live trades and the inability to predict which level holds are stated as the invalidation of using such levels for stops.
claims.source_timeframe_or_horizon_if_explicit: intraday ('at the end of the day') as the example context

claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: No one will ever provide you with a quantitative proof of Fibonacci levels working. ... I have yet to receive a single shred of actual work done on these ratios. ... I place no emphasis at all on Fibonacci levels. Here's the real key: you do not need them.
claims.source_failure_or_counterexample_anchor: Absence of quantitative proof is treated as the counterevidence to Fibonacci usage.

claims.ambiguity_notes: 'About 50%' and 'very large margin of error' are intentionally imprecise; the swing definition and measurement method are not specified by the source.

claims.source_applicability_if_explicit: Stated as a simple data-supported replacement for Fibonacci retracement levels.
claims.source_context_note: Closing paragraph referencing the author's quantitative posts on Fibonacci. 'about 50% with a very large margin of error' is the source's own qualitative description and must not be sharpened into a precise threshold.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: No, this is not, nor is it intended to be, a disproof of the theory, but it does offer a simple replacement that is supported by the data: look for retracements to end at about 50% of the previous swing, with a very large margin of error. We might wish for more precision, but that is all I have been able to find in the data. Good news, though: it's enough.

claims.source_context_note: Bullet on randomness. The source describes experiential learning about perception and pattern-finding in random data.
claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: I generated many charts of random market data according to various techniques and spent a lot of time looking at them. ... when you see how easily your perception is swayed and how easily you find patterns in random data, you start to think deeply. Does it invalidate the idea of patterns in real market data? Of course not, but it certainly challenges the claims of 'just look at a chart! You can see it works!'
claims.source_invalidation_if_explicit: Challenges visual 'just look at a chart' evidence claims, without invalidating patterns in real data.

claims.source_excerpt_short_or_paraphrase: Much of the discipline of technical analysis rests on the idea that people have a memory around specific prices. ... there are different ways that historical charts must be adjusted. With futures, there are at least three common methods (difference, ratio, or unadjusted), and the question of when to roll to new contracts. ... The answer I got from asking many people was either confusion or 'it doesn't matter.'
